subject: geography

questions.content: What is the minimum sea surface temperature usually needed for a tropical storm to form?
questions.explanation: Warm water provides the heat and moisture that power the storm.

questions.content: In the north-west Pacific Ocean, a tropical storm is called a
questions.explanation: Hurricane is used in the Atlantic and north-east Pacific, typhoon in the north-west Pacific, and cyclone in the Indian and south Pacific oceans.

questions.content: What is the calm, clear centre of a tropical storm called?
questions.explanation: The eye has sinking air and light winds. The eyewall around it has the strongest winds and heaviest rain.

questions.content: A storm surge is
options: A very large wave caused by an earthquake
A rise in sea level caused by strong winds and low pressure pushing water towards the coast
A heavy shower in the mountains
A slow tide on a calm day
questions.explanation: Storm surges often cause the most deaths in tropical storms because of coastal flooding.

questions.content: Which is the main cause of river flooding?
options: More water enters the river than its channel can hold, for example after prolonged or intense rain
questions.explanation: Flooding occurs when discharge exceeds channel capacity.

questions.content: Why do tropical storms lose strength when they move over land?
options: The land is warmer than the sea
The air over land is moister
They are cut off from the warm ocean water that supplies their energy
questions.explanation: Heat and moisture from the sea power the storm. Friction with land also slows the winds.

questions.content: Hurricane Katrina struck the US Gulf Coast in August 2005. Which factor made the flooding in New Orleans so severe?
options: Storm surge and failures of levees (flood walls) protecting a city partly below sea level
questions.explanation: Much of New Orleans lies below sea level and the levees failed in several places, flooding large areas.

questions.content: Why are tropical storms rarely seen close to the Equator?
options: The Coriolis effect is too weak there to make the storm spin
questions.explanation: Coriolis force is needed to give the spin. It is zero at the Equator, so storms form at least about 5° away.

questions.content: Typhoon Haiyan hit the Philippines in November 2013. Which impact was most severe?
options: A powerful storm surge and winds destroyed coastal communities, with more than 6,000 deaths
A drought across the whole country
questions.explanation: Haiyan was one of the strongest tropical cyclones recorded at landfall, and the storm surge was especially deadly in Tacloban.

questions.content: Which factor increases flood risk in an urban area?
options: Large areas of impermeable surfaces like roads and roofs that speed up run-off
questions.explanation: Concrete and tarmac stop infiltration, so rain reaches rivers faster, giving a short lag time and higher peak flow.

questions.content: A river's peak discharge rose from 80 m³/s to 140 m³/s after heavy rain. What was the percentage increase?
questions.explanation: Increase 60 ÷ 80 × 100 = 75%. 43% divides by the new value.

questions.content: Which is an example of SOFT engineering to reduce flood risk?
options: Afforestation in the upper catchment and floodplain zoning
questions.explanation: Soft engineering works with natural processes. Walls, dredging and dams are hard engineering.

questions.content: In Bangladesh, a cyclone preparedness programme uses volunteers, warning flags and shelters. What impact has this had?
options: Deaths from major cyclones have fallen greatly compared with the 1970 Bhola cyclone
It replaces the need for shelters
questions.explanation: The Bhola cyclone killed an estimated several hundred thousand people. Better warnings and shelters have cut loss of life in later storms.

questions.content: In 2022 severe monsoon flooding in Pakistan affected tens of millions of people. Which combination of causes is most accurate?
options: Extremely heavy monsoon rain together with glacier melt, and vulnerable low-lying communities
questions.explanation: Floods had natural causes but human vulnerability such as poverty and poor infrastructure increased the impact.

questions.content: Two coastal towns face the same storm. Town A has a sea wall, shelters and an early-warning system. Town B has none. Which statement best explains the likely difference in impact?
options: The hazard is different in each town
Town A has lower vulnerability and greater capacity to cope, so losses should be smaller
Town A will be hit harder because it has a wall
questions.explanation: The hazard is the same but risk depends on vulnerability and capacity to cope.

questions.content: A government must choose between building a 10 km flood wall (high cost, protects one city) and restoring wetlands and reforesting a catchment (lower cost, slower benefit, wider effects). Which judgement is most balanced?
options: The wall is perfect and needs no maintenance
The wall protects quickly but may fail and shift flooding downstream; catchment restoration is cheaper and sustainable but slower, so a combination may be best
Neither option can reduce flood risk
questions.explanation: Good evaluation compares speed, cost, sustainability, who benefits and who may lose.

questions.content: A student claims: 'Because a hurricane caused fewer deaths in a rich country than a similar storm in a poor country, the storm in the rich country was weaker.' What is the best critique?
options: Death tolls depend on vulnerability, preparation and response, so they do not measure storm strength alone
Death tolls are exactly equal to storm strength
Poor countries do not have warnings
questions.explanation: Hazard strength and disaster impact are different. Compare wind speed, surge height and exposure as well.

questions.content: Evaluate whether climate change will make tropical storm disasters worse.
options: It will certainly make every storm stronger and nothing else matters
Climate change has no connection with seas
Storms depend only on land temperature
Warmer seas may increase storm intensity and rainfall and rising sea levels raise surge risk, but the impact also depends on population growth in coastal areas and preparedness
questions.explanation: Strong answers distinguish the hazard from the disaster, mention both physical and human factors and acknowledge uncertainty about storm frequency.

note:
Weather hazards are extreme events such as tropical storms, floods, droughts and wildfires. A **hazard** is a natural event that could cause harm; a **disaster** happens when a hazard seriously affects people, property or the environment. A hurricane over empty ocean is a hazard but not a disaster.

## Tropical storms
A tropical storm is an intense low-pressure system with strong winds and heavy rain. They are called hurricanes in the Atlantic and north-east Pacific, typhoons in the north-west Pacific and cyclones in the Indian and south Pacific oceans.

Conditions for formation:
- sea surface temperature of about 26.5°C or more, over a depth of tens of metres
- a location at least about 5° from the Equator, so the Coriolis effect can make the storm spin
- low wind shear, so the storm can grow upright
Warm moist air rises, condenses and releases heat, which drives more rising air. The centre, the **eye**, has sinking air and calm weather; the **eyewall** around it has the strongest winds. Storms weaken over land or cold water because they lose their energy source.

## Impacts
Primary impacts include destroyed buildings and deaths from strong winds and flooding. The **storm surge**, a rise in sea level driven by wind and low pressure, is often the deadliest part. Secondary impacts include disease, loss of jobs and long-term economic damage. Hurricane Katrina (August 2005) flooded much of New Orleans after levees failed. Typhoon Haiyan (November 2013) devastated parts of the Philippines, with more than 6,000 deaths, mostly from the surge. Bangladesh has reduced deaths since the Bhola cyclone of 1970 by building shelters, using volunteers and issuing warnings.

## Floods
River floods occur when more water enters a river than the channel can carry. Causes:
- physical: heavy or prolonged rain, snowmelt, steep impermeable catchments
- human: deforestation, urbanisation with impermeable surfaces, poor drainage and building on floodplains
Pakistan's 2022 monsoon floods, which affected tens of millions of people, combined extreme rain, glacier melt and vulnerable communities.

## Managing floods
- **Hard engineering**: flood walls, levees, dams and channel straightening. Effective locally but expensive and can move flooding downstream.
- **Soft engineering**: afforestation, wetland restoration, floodplain zoning and flood warnings. Often cheaper and more sustainable, but slower.
Warnings only work if people receive them and know what to do.

## Hazard, vulnerability and risk
Risk depends on the hazard, how vulnerable people are, and their capacity to cope. This is why a similar storm can cause very different results in different places. Poverty, poor housing and weak governance increase vulnerability.

## Percentage change practice
Peak discharge rising from 80 to 140 m³/s is an increase of 60 ÷ 80 × 100 = 75%. Always divide by the starting value.

## How this is examined
You may get a storm track map, a hydrograph or a short news article. You describe patterns, explain causes, compare impacts in countries at different income levels and evaluate management. Link physical processes to human choices.

Exam tip: Separate the hazard from the disaster. A strong answer says the storm was the same strength but the impact differed because of vulnerability and preparation.

flashcards.back: Sea surface at about 26.5°C or more, at least about 5° from the Equator for Coriolis spin, and low wind shear.
Same type of storm: hurricane (Atlantic, NE Pacific), typhoon (NW Pacific), cyclone (Indian and S Pacific).
Eye: calm centre with sinking air. Eyewall: ring of strongest winds and heaviest rain.
A rise in sea level from wind and low pressure pushing water ashore; often the deadliest effect of a tropical storm.
A hazard is a natural event that could cause harm. A disaster occurs when it causes serious loss to people.
Heavy rain, snowmelt, impermeable surfaces, deforestation, urbanisation and building on floodplains.
Hard: walls, levees, dams. Soft: afforestation, wetlands, zoning, warnings. Soft is often cheaper and more sustainable.
Storm surge and levee failure flooded New Orleans, which is partly below sea level.
Depends on hazard, vulnerability and capacity to cope. High vulnerability and low capacity raise risk.

subject: geography

questions.content: What is a drought?
options: A prolonged period of below-average rainfall causing water shortage
questions.explanation: Droughts develop slowly and last weeks, months or years, and can affect farming, water supplies and ecosystems.

questions.content: Which of the following is a main ingredient of a wildfire?
options: Fuel such as dry vegetation, heat or an ignition source, and oxygen
questions.explanation: Fire needs fuel, heat and oxygen. Dry vegetation, high temperatures and wind make wildfires spread.

questions.content: A drought that reduces soil moisture and harms crop growth is called
questions.explanation: Meteorological drought = lack of rain. Agricultural drought = effects on crops. Hydrological drought = low rivers and reservoirs.

questions.content: Which of these increases the risk of wildfires?
options: Hot, dry, windy weather and a build-up of dead vegetation
questions.explanation: Dry fuel ignites easily and wind carries flames and embers quickly.

questions.content: Which is a good example of a firebreak?
options: A cleared strip of land that stops flames spreading
questions.explanation: Firebreaks remove fuel to slow or stop the fire's advance.

questions.content: Between 2020 and 2023 several rainy seasons in a row failed across the Horn of Africa. What was the most serious consequence?
options: A rise in river flooding everywhere
Crop failure and livestock deaths led to severe food insecurity for millions of people
questions.explanation: Prolonged drought in pastoral and farming areas caused hunger and displacement, worsened by high food prices and conflict.

questions.content: Australia's 'Black Summer' bushfires of 2019-20 burned about 18 million hectares. Which factor helped create these conditions?
options: Record heat and a long drought left vegetation extremely dry
questions.explanation: Prolonged drought and heat dried the fuel. Strong winds then spread fires, and smoke affected many cities.

questions.content: The Camp Fire in California (November 2018) destroyed the town of Paradise and killed 85 people. Which lesson is most strongly linked to this disaster?
options: Wildfires can only happen in tropical regions
Communities near forests need effective evacuation plans, warning systems and fire-safe design
Fires are always started by lightning
questions.explanation: Rapid fire spread, narrow roads and limited warning time showed the importance of planning for evacuation.

questions.content: Which human activity can contribute to the spread of wildfire risk?
options: Building homes in forested areas and starting fires carelessly
Reducing the amount of dry vegetation
questions.explanation: More people near fire-prone vegetation increases both ignition sources and property exposed to fire.

questions.content: Reservoir storage in a city fell from 600 million m³ to 270 million m³ during a drought. What percentage of storage was lost?
questions.explanation: Loss = 330. 330 ÷ 600 × 100 = 55%. 45% is the percentage that remains.

questions.content: Which of these is a short-term response to drought?
options: Water restrictions and emergency food aid
questions.explanation: Short-term responses address immediate needs. Reservoirs, new crops and legislation are long-term.

questions.content: Which is an example of a long-term drought adaptation?
options: Importing emergency water for a week
Developing drought-resistant crops and efficient irrigation
questions.explanation: Adaptation reduces vulnerability over time, for example by changing crops and improving water storage.

questions.content: Disaster risk can be described as depending on hazard, vulnerability and capacity to cope. Which action mainly increases capacity to cope?
options: Training communities and building emergency shelters and stores
Building more homes on a floodplain
questions.explanation: Capacity to cope includes skills, resources, institutions and preparedness.

questions.content: The Sendai Framework (2015-2030) is an international agreement that aims to
options: Reduce disaster risk and losses by improving understanding of risk, governance and preparedness
questions.explanation: It sets priorities for countries to reduce disaster losses rather than preventing hazards.

questions.content: A town has one road out and is surrounded by dry forest. A resident says: 'Spending on forest clearing, warning sirens and evacuation drills is wasted because fires cannot be stopped.' What is the best response?
options: The resident is right since hazards cannot be altered
The measures will stop all fires
These measures cannot stop fires but can reduce deaths and damage by lowering vulnerability and improving response
questions.explanation: Risk reduction does not remove the hazard, but it reduces the impact. Evidence supports preparedness.

questions.content: Compare two droughts of similar rainfall deficit. Country P has irrigation, crop insurance and grain stores. Country Q relies on rain-fed farming and has no reserves. Which prediction is most reasonable?
options: Country Q will suffer more severe food shortages because it is more vulnerable
Country P will be hit harder
questions.explanation: Impact depends on vulnerability and resilience as well as the hazard. Safety nets reduce losses.

questions.content: A region's wildfire frequency has doubled over 30 years. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Several factors, such as climate warming, land-use change and fire management, may be involved and should be examined
It must be caused only by arsonists
It cannot be explained at all
questions.explanation: Wildfire trends result from interacting factors. Good geography avoids single-cause explanations.

questions.content: Evaluate: 'Governments should spend more on preparing for hazards than on responding after they happen.'
options: Preparation is useless because disasters are random
Only the poorest countries should prepare
Preparedness usually costs less than recovery and saves lives, but responses are still needed for unavoidable events, so a balance is wise
questions.explanation: Studies of disaster risk reduction suggest investment in prevention gives high returns, but no system removes all risk.

note:
Droughts and wildfires are weather hazards that develop and spread differently from storms. Droughts are slow-onset hazards; wildfires can spread in minutes. This sub-topic also pulls together how societies reduce the risk from all weather hazards.

## Droughts
A **drought** is a prolonged period of lower-than-normal rainfall that causes water shortage. We distinguish:
- **meteorological** drought: lack of rain
- **agricultural** drought: soil moisture too low for crops
- **hydrological** drought: rivers, lakes and reservoirs fall low
Causes include shifts in atmospheric circulation, natural climate cycles such as El Niño, and long-term climate change. Human factors such as over-extraction of water make impacts worse.

Impacts include crop failure, livestock deaths, food shortages and higher prices, water restrictions, wildfires, migration and sometimes conflict. The Horn of Africa suffered several failed rainy seasons in a row from 2020, and millions faced severe hunger. Responses can be short-term (water restrictions, food aid) and long-term (drought-resistant crops, efficient irrigation, rainwater harvesting, new storage and better forecasting).

## Wildfires
Wildfires need **fuel**, **heat** and **oxygen**. Hot, dry and windy weather dries vegetation and spreads flames. Causes can be natural (lightning) or human (campfires, power lines, arson). Impacts include loss of life, homes and wildlife, air pollution and carbon emissions, and soil erosion afterwards. In Australia's 2019-20 "Black Summer", fires burned about 18 million hectares after record heat and drought. The Camp Fire in California in 2018 destroyed the town of Paradise and killed 85 people, showing the danger when many people live near flammable vegetation and have little warning.

Management: firebreaks and controlled burns to reduce fuel, fire-resistant building design, early detection using satellites, warning and evacuation plans, and public education.

## Disaster risk reduction
Risk depends on the **hazard**, how **vulnerable** people are and their **capacity to cope**. Reducing risk means lowering vulnerability and raising capacity, since we often cannot stop the hazard. Common approaches:
- **Predict**: monitoring and forecasting
- **Protect**: engineering and land-use planning
- **Prepare**: drills, shelters, stores and insurance
- **Plan for recovery**: funding, rebuilding and learning
The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015-2030) sets international goals to cut disaster losses.

Wealth is important but not everything. Well-organised communities with good warning systems, such as in Bangladesh, can protect people even where incomes are low.

## Analysing data
A reservoir falling from 600 to 270 million m³ has lost (600 − 270) ÷ 600 × 100 = 55%. Check the base value and say clearly what the percentage refers to. When asked about trends in wildfires or droughts, avoid assuming one cause; consider climate, land use and management together.

## How this is examined
Tasks give a news report or a graph of rainfall and reservoir levels. You identify type and causes of a hazard, calculate changes, assess impacts on different groups and recommend or evaluate risk-reduction strategies.

Common mistakes: confusing hazard with disaster; blaming a single cause; assuming that hard engineering is always best; giving only short-term responses.

Exam tip: Match each strategy to its time scale and stakeholder, then judge which gives the best balance of cost, effectiveness and sustainability.
